artifacts.rejected_response:
The adjudication of such disputes begins with a shared analytical vocabulary. Taphonomy is the study of the processes that affect remains between death and recovery, and it supplies the null hypothesis against which any claim of deliberate mortuary behavior must be tested: gravity, water, sediment creep, scavengers, and roof collapse can all assemble bones into configurations that superficially resemble graves. The burden therefore falls on the ritual reading, which must demonstrate features that no combination of ordinary agencies would be expected to produce.

Anthropologists inspect sediment stratigraphy for the outline of a dug pit when testing a burial hypothesis, and it was that inspection which produced the result reported for this deposit, namely that a grave cut was identified in the sediment profile surrounding the remains. Only one other outcome was available: that no grave cut was identified in that profile. The two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold, which is why the stratigraphic reading is decisive rather than merely suggestive. The identification is further supported by a standard criterion of field practice, since sediment inside a suspected grave that differs in texture from the surrounding matrix is treated as evidence of infilling, and precisely such a textural contrast confirms the cut recorded here.

Micromorphology involves examining intact blocks of sediment in thin section under a microscope, a procedure that resolves fabric relationships invisible in the trench wall. In one such application, micromorphological analysis flagged sediment disturbance consistent with a dug feature. At least one of two independent results obtains at this locality: that micromorphological finding, or the outcome of the geometric approach, in which spatial statistical analysis flagged a bone distribution inconsistent with natural accumulation. One or both must be granted for the excavators' case to have any purchase.

The condition of the skeleton itself carries comparable weight. The articulation of the skeletal elements indicates that the body was covered while its joints were still held by soft tissue; in other words, the preserved joint relationships show that interment happened before decomposition disarticulated the corpse. Against this stand the diagnostic signatures of the competing account. Carnivore tooth marks and gnawing damage on bone point to scavenger involvement in an accumulation, and because such involvement is present, water transport of skeletal elements tends to sort bones by size and density. That sorting pattern in turn confirms the articulation reading described above, since the joints of a body covered while soft tissue survived would resist such reorganization. Cultural indicators are then marshaled in a fixed sequence of argument: grave goods placed in contact with a body are cited as evidence of intentional deposition, and only after that appeal has been entered is ochre staining on human remains used to argue for symbolic treatment of the dead. The order in which these two appeals are conventionally made reflects reporting custom alone and licenses no inference from the first to the second.

The Rising Star cave system in South Africa produced Homo naledi fossils beginning in 2013. Later, as a matter of chronology and not of consequence, Lee Berger and colleagues argued that Homo naledi deliberately interred bodies in the Dinaledi Chamber. Although they advanced that interpretation, critics of the Homo naledi burial claim proposed gravity-driven sediment movement and a natural death trap as alternative explanations, and the dispute could not be resolved by appeal to the field observations alone. What settled the matter procedurally was the judgment of the reviewers at eLife, who concluded that the evidence presented for deliberate burial by Homo naledi was incomplete. That verdict shows how such disagreements are closed in practice: not by the intuitive plausibility of ritual, but by whether the stratigraphic, micromorphological, and articulation criteria have been documented to a standard that excludes the taphonomic alternative.

artifacts.rejected_response:
Adjudication in cases of this kind proceeds not by intuition about whether a
stone "looks worked" but by testing the fracture morphology of an assemblage
against the depositional energy of the beds that contained it. The Calico Early
Man Site, which lies in the Calico Hills of the central Mojave Desert in San
Bernardino County, California, remains the standard illustration of how such a
test is conducted and of how it can fail to produce consensus. Excavation there
began in 1964 under the field direction of Ruth DeEtte Simpson. Louis Leakey
served as a director of the project, and his involvement gave the work an
international profile that few desert excavations attain. The chipped stones
were recovered from alluvial fan deposits assigned to the Yermo Formation — a
stratigraphic placement that holds provided that the excavation was indeed
opened in 1964 under Simpson's field direction.

The chronological stakes explain the intensity of the dispute. Uranium-series
determinations on carbonates at the site returned ages on the order of 200,000
years; the conventional model, by contrast, places the earliest widely accepted
human occupation of the region at roughly 13,000 years ago. An artifactual
interpretation of the Yermo material would therefore not refine the accepted
sequence but overturn it by more than an order of magnitude, which is precisely
why the burden of demonstration falls on the excavators rather than on their
critics.

The analytical apparatus brought to bear is morphological in the first
instance. Analysts rely on conchoidal fracture features such as striking
platforms and bulbs of percussion to identify intentional flaking. Specifically,
Alfred Barnes proposed that a platform-flake angle of less than ninety degrees
indicates deliberate percussion, a quantitative threshold that can be applied
uniformly across a large sample. Tumbling-barrel experiments on unworked rock
produce pseudo-tools that resemble struck flakes, and it was this experimental
result that drove analysts to adopt the conchoidal criteria in the first place,
since a diagnostic capable of separating percussion from abrasion was needed
once mechanical mimicry had been demonstrated.

Applied to Calico, these procedures yielded a negative verdict. Critics
classified the Calico specimens as geofacts. Vance Haynes attributed the
flake-like breakage to high-energy transport of cobbles within a debris flow,
which indicates that the geofact classification rests on an identified
mechanism rather than on mere skepticism about age. At least one of two
independent lines of inquiry — attribute analysis of platform angles and flake
scars, or sedimentological analysis of the depositional energy of the fan —
flagged the specimens as consistent with natural breakage, and quite possibly
both did. The sedimentological result is, in other words, simply Haynes's
debris-flow attribution restated in the vocabulary of transport energy: the same
claim about cobbles battered in a high-energy flow, expressed as a property of
the deposit rather than of the stones.

Institutional review was the mechanism through which these competing readings
were finally weighed. An international conference of specialists was convened in
1970 to inspect the Calico excavation and its collections. Reports of what the
visitors concluded diverge irreconcilably: either every specimen recovered from
the deposit was accepted as human-made by the visiting reviewers, or at least
one specimen was judged by them to be a product of natural fracture. Both
descriptions cannot be true, and one of them must be. Louis Leakey maintained
that the Calico objects were human-made until his death in 1972, even though the
reviewers had judged at least one specimen to be naturally fractured. That
tension is settled by the documentary record: the final report of the 1970
international conference, issued after the specialists' inspection of the site
and its collections, concluded that the Calico specimens were the products of
natural fracturing. Leakey's position was thus a dissent from a recorded
collective judgment, and the general lesson is that extraordinary antiquity
claims are resolved by demonstrating that the enclosing sediments could not have
produced the observed breakage, not by cataloguing specimens that resemble
tools.
